title: Learned forecasts distinguish directional search and COVID-data relationships
summary: Matched LightGBM forecasts of eight Google-search and COVID-related series found that opposite directions could differ in both prediction error and error-distribution behavior. For US loss-of-smell searches and reported cases, adding search history gave a 9.9% equivalent mean RMSE reduction, while the reverse direction changed error-distribution descriptors without improving mean accuracy. These are model-dependent observational patterns, not causal effects or a validated real-time warning system.
organization: Petrozavodsk State University; University of Manouba

source_review.scope: Original v1 front, computational Methods, application Results and limitations; no independent reproduction

evidence.tested: Each 400-day window used 14-day histories, one- to fourteen-day horizons and chronological 223-origin training/150-origin evaluation. Target-only and source-augmented branches shared settings. Results Tables 6 and 9 separate mean log-RMSE and forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE).
evidence.unknown: Adjacent windows share 399 days and are not independent replications. Window/history settings were chosen sequentially for distributional stability. Relative Google Trends sampling, query wording, common media/seasonal/reporting effects and the fixed model class limit interpretation. No temporally constrained surrogate-source null test was included. Similar broad lead-lag findings were known; the represented refinement is the matched metric-dependent directional contrast, not the discovery that searches can precede cases.
evidence.ai_role: Learned tree ensembles generate matched conditional forecasts whose held-out errors reveal the source- and direction-specific contrast; FEDE itself is a statistical descriptor, not a separate learned model.
